Purple-spotted bigeye (Priacanthus tayenus) is a commercially important species distributed throughout the tropical and subtropical waters of the Indo-West Pacific. Recent growth studies based on otolith increment analysis of specimens collected from trawl surveys off the coast of Thailand indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded fork length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a size consistent with the upper range observed among members of the family Priacanthidae. The length-weight relationship derived from these individuals suggests that an adult of this ultimate length corresponds to a wet body mass of 642.4 grams [Wwi = 642.4 grams], reflecting a moderately deep-bodied morphology typical of bigeyes. Field data from the Gulf of Thailand further show that the fork length at which 50 percent of the population has attained sexual maturity is 21.1 cm [Lp = 21.1 cm], a value obtained through macroscopic examination of gonad condition across a large sample of individuals. This length at puberty is slightly larger than values reported for the related congener Priacanthus macracanthus, suggesting a relatively delayed onset of reproductive activity in Purple-spotted bigeye.

Reproductive output in Priacanthus tayenus has been characterised through laboratory-based spawning trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], gravid females were observed to release clutches containing approximately 672 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 672 eggs per spawning event], with a mean spawning frequency of slightly less than one event per day [F_R_i = slightly less than one event per day] during the peak reproductive season. This implies a substantial daily fecundity for a fish of this body size consistent with an r-selected life-history strategy adapted to variable environmental conditions in tropical shelf habitats.

The early life stages of Purple-spotted bigeye are characterised by a small initial size at birth, reflecting a strategy of producing numerous pelagic offspring. Based on field samples of newly emerged larvae, the wet weight at birth of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva was measured at approximately 0.000074 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000074 grams], a value that places the prolarvae among the smallest of the family Priacanthidae and reflects the energetic constraints of producing large numbers of pelagic eggs. Following yolk-sac resorption, which typically occurs within two to three days post-hatching at 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the free-swimming larvae initiate exogenous feeding on small copepod nauplii. The exotrophic transition is a critical period, with larval survival heavily dependent on the match between first feeding and the availability of suitable planktonic prey.

Growth trajectories derived from mark-recapture studies indicate that puberty corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 148 grams [Wwp = approximately 148 grams] for both sexes, a value predicted from the length-weight relationship using the observed fork length at maturity of 21.1 cm. This body mass at the onset of gonadal maturation represents roughly 23 percent of the theoretical ultimate wet weight of 642.4 grams [Wwi = 642.4 grams], suggesting that individuals invest in reproduction well before achieving their maximum somatic size. Such an early investment in reproductive effort is commonly observed in species with relatively high natural mortality rates, where early reproduction is favoured over extended somatic growth to ensure some lifetime reproductive success.

Longevity estimates for Priacanthus tayenus, derived from the examination of sectioned otoliths from over 200 individuals, place the maximum lifespan at 10 years [am = 10 years] for fish maintained under natural temperature regimes averaging 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], a duration that corresponds to a relatively modest lifespan for a teleost of this ultimate body size when compared to longer-lived members of the family such as Priacanthus arenatus. The observed mortality patterns show that senescence-related declines in condition begin after roughly eight years, with very few individuals surviving beyond the tenth year in the wild. This lifespan, combined with the species' high reproductive output of almost one spawning event per day [F_R_i = almost one spawning event per day] each yielding approximately 672 eggs [N_R_i = each yielding approximately 672 eggs], results in a lifetime fecundity that can exceed several million eggs per female.
